title: Barcodes, the scanner and the discount label
summary: Supermarket Simulator makes the barcode an object rather than a marking: the game spawns one for a product, lets you drag it onto the scanner, and keeps a second, green label for discounted goods.
body: In this shop a barcode is a thing you handle rather than a marking printed on the box. The game has a barcode object, a spawner that produces it and a way of dragging it, which is why scanning is an action you take rather than a menu choice you make.
The scanner is a device of its own. It has its own interaction and its own networked version, so in a shared shop the game can show one player scanning without letting the other do it by accident.
A hint handler tells you what the scanner expects. The same device keeps a helper for its input hint, which is how the game prompts you at the till rather than leaving you to guess at a button.

Scanning produces a sale item. What you scan is recorded as a sale item on the scanner rather than quietly changing a total, which is why an item that went through wrongly can still be dealt with before the customer pays.

Discounts have a barcode of their own. The game ships a second label picture for discounted goods, and the discount side of the shop has a manager and a panel of its own, so a reduced product is not simply the ordinary label with a smaller number behind it.

The scale shares the same work. One of the game's task records applies a barcode at the scale, so weighing a loose item and scanning a packaged one belong to the same flow rather than two separate jobs.

The till itself is a set of named parts: a belt, a belt grid, a drawer, a change manager and a screen, and a checkout carries a type, which is how the game tells an ordinary till from the self-service one.
The two labels beside this entry are the game's own: the one it spawns for a product and the green one it keeps for discounted goods.
What this entry does not tell you: how the digits on the label are generated, what they mean, or how a discount is calculated. We have not verified those, so we do not print them.

facts.claim: A barcode is an object the game spawns, with a spawner and a way of dragging it.
The scanner is a device with its own interaction and a networked version.
The game keeps a helper that tells you what input the scanner expects.
What is scanned is recorded as a sale item rather than only changing a total.
The game ships a second label picture for discounted goods, and discounts have a manager and a panel.
One of the game's task records applies a barcode at the scale.
The build has a handler for the animation a scan plays.
A till is made of named parts, and a checkout carries a type.
facts.evidence: identifiers: CheckoutBelt, CheckoutBeltGrid, CheckoutDrawer, CheckoutChangeManager, CheckoutType

facts.claim: Barcodes are drawn from their own pieces: a barcode material with an icon, a background for that icon and a shadow, plus a barcode of its own for produce.
facts.evidence: asset names: M_Barcode, M_Barcode_Icon, M_Barcode_Icon_BG, M_Barcode_Shadow, T_Barcode_Vegie
